utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is in session. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. I'd like to greet the Defence, General Tolimir, Mr. Gajic, the OTP, Mr. Vanderpuye, and his associate, and all the people assisting us in and around this courtroom. As you may have noticed, the Presiding Judge is not here today. He is away for medical reasons. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Your Honour. Mr. Tolimir is having some technical problems with his headphones. He is not receiving any sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The usher will check what the matter is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been solved, Mr. President. We apologise for this interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I said that, pursuant to Rule 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that it can sit as is fit, pursuant to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and in light of the seniority of the Judges here, I have the honour to be the Presiding Judge today. We shall continue with the examination-in-chief of the Prosecutor this morning, Mr. Vanderpuye, but prior to that, we shall bring the witness in the courtroom, and we need to move into closed session. Registrar, please, closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We are in open session once again. Good morning, Witness. Witness, Zoran Malinic, let me remind you that the statement you gave yesterday to tell the truth and nothing but the truth, the solemn declaration that you gave today, still applies today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: I shall give to the floor to the Prosecutor, Mr. Vanderpuye, for the rest of his examination-in-chief. Mr. Vanderpuye, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Good morning to you, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good morning to you, Mr. Malinic. We had yesterday P663B, I believe, which was the intercept in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could continue with that, please. And if we could please go to the next page in the English, and I think we stay on the same page in the B/C/S. It's a bit difficult to see here. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I had begun asking you, sir, about the conversation that continues with Beara and Zoka, and you will notice in the middle of the page in the English, and I think just about the middle also in the B/C/S, you'll see a reference to, "About 500." It says: "What's new?" Beara says: "What's new?" And the answer is: "Well easy, there are about 500." After that, you'll see that Beara says: "Excellent, man." Zoka says: "At least it looks like 20. One group got through during the night up there, behind our backs." The reference to the group that got through during that night, is that a reference to the night of the 12th, into the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this conversation took place at quarter past 10.00, as it says here, I suppose it happened the previous night, between the 12th and 13th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So from this intercept, it's clear that there were groups moving through that area on the night of the 12th, at least into the 13th.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to greet all those present and may peace be in this house and these proceedings completed in keeping with God's will and not my own. I'd like to greet Mr. Malinic and wish him a pleasant stay. When this document was shown to him yesterday, he said that he couldn't see people in Kasaba because it was 8 kilometres away. Now we have another reference here. There's a mention of a night and some people who went behind someone's back. Is it a group from Kasaba or some other group? It seems that things got mixed up here during this electronic intercept. It seems now he's -- it's not clear whether he is talking about Kasaba or Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think that the answer that the witness has given is clear, given the context in which this intercept arises. We have before us the transcript from yesterday. The conversation began with Mr. Lucic, Captain Lucic, the witness's deputy. The conversation specifically concerned 400, as Beara put it, balijas, in the area of Konjevic Polje, and this is simply the continuation of that same conversation. So I think the context is clear from the intercept itself. And certainly if General Tolimir wants to know more about the intercept, he's welcome to do that when he cross-examines the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to Mr. Vanderpuye. I don't want to ask the witness anything at all about this intercept. I just asked the Prosecutor, given the fact that he is tendering documents about two locations, one of which was 8 kilometres away, and the other was Kasaba. Did he do this on purpose, or does one conversation stem from another? This is what I wanted to ask the Prosecutor, not the Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, perhaps we could have more information on the part of the witness, because I believe that he took part in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. And that's exactly where I'm going with this document. But it takes a little time to get there. I can't do it instantly in one question. And that's the reason why I've asked the questions in the order and in the sequence that I have. If I can proceed, maybe we can clarify this as we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, you see here a reference to 500. This is immediately after Beara gets you on the line. He says: "Hi, Zoka." And then it says: "What's new?" And you say: "Well easy, there are about 500." You see that in the intercept? Should be about midway through.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then I asked you about this reference here to one group got through during the night. First let me ask you, at about 10.00 in the morning, what was the estimate that you got from the people that you sent out earlier that day as to how many people were in the vicinity in the hills that were coming down to surrender? You said you sent three people out and they brought back prisoners, and they told you that they were a large group of soldiers, I believe you said, in the hills. How many did they tell you were there, around that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to correct something you said. You said I sent out three soldiers, and yesterday I said I had sent a group of five soldiers, if I remember correctly, who came back with three prisoners. It was around 6.30 or 7.00, although I can't recall exactly when I sent the group out and at what time the prisoners were brought in; that is to say, the first three prisoners brought to the barracks. The assessment of the first group I sent to reconnoitre was that there were many, as many as several hundred along that route. They saw them crossing the road between Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So what you see here are 500, is that inconsistent with what you were told by the five -- or one of the five soldiers that you sent out earlier that morning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not inconsistent with it. They said there were several hundred. If this conversation took place at 10.15, as recorded here, this entails a different situation. It's a different time in relation to the time I received this original piece of information. If that group at 6.30 or 7.00 in the morning on the 13th said that there were several hundred, then the time we are discussing, at 10.15, is already a different time and the number of people may well have changed in that area. Those were all assessments. It was impossible, due to the terrain they were in, to see how many exactly there were. It was also because of the direction from which the forces of the 28th Division came. It was for that reason that we -- we could not assess how many forces they had at their disposal during their breakthrough to Cerska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Prosecutor. Registrar, I believe that the document we have on the screen should not be broadcast. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that correct. This document is confidential and should not be broadcast. Aside from that, it can be discussed in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this document may be displayed on the screen inside the courtroom but not broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let's go to the next page in the English, please. And I think we will have to go to the next page in the B/C/S also.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You see at the top of the page in the English: "They're close to 200." And that immediately follows a remark about Konjevic Polje. Beara says: "Yes." And then he says: "About 200, right, got through?" And you say: "Yes, yes. And it's like, like they're in groups of five to six or four." And he says: "Uh-huh, okay." Do you see that, first of all, in the intercept?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does it comport with your memory, your recollection of the events?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I be allowed to read the part before and immediately after this so as to have the entire context and to be able to provide a more precise answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's do that then. We'll go to the previous page in the English. And I think we'll probably be on the same page in the B/C/S. But you can see this conversation unfolds after there's a reference to the group that goes through during the night. Beara says: "Uh-huh." And then it says -- there's an unclear part where you say: "Forces to come, so we could resolve this problem ..." He says: "Yes, yes." And then there's some colloquy that's unheard. And you say: "... they're killing ..." And he says: "Well excellent. Just let them continue ..." You say: "That's it. That's the situation ..." And then it says: "Bye ..." He says: "Hey." And you say: "Konjevic Polje." And then it continues, as I've just mentioned, about the 200 getting through in groups of five, six, and four, that we see on the next page. Does that help put things in context for you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we should continue. It says: "Well, I am going to tell those in Zvornik." I suppose it meant that, to my left, I had set up a blockade line with the forces I had available, but it did not close the gap. And there was still an area that was not covered to my left, if I faced the enemy; that is to say, between Nova Kasaba and Konjevic Polje. That area was not cut off. And it was because of that that such groups could freely get through. That is how I understand this part of the conversation. I apologise. When you were reading a moment ago, when you mentioned what I said, not killing but killing themselves, and there are many wounded. And then Beara asked me, What? They're killing each other? And I didn't receive that part of the intercept, at least not in my language.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you another intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's P2205.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise. While we still have this intercept on the screen, Mr. Vanderpuye should clear something up. Now we have a third situation in one conversation. First, it was Konjevic Polje, then Nova Kasaba, and now it seems we have a third person participating. So is this a compilation of three conversations or are these the same collocutors all the way through?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, I believe this is an important clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. At the beginning of the intercept we can see clearly that the collocutors are Beara and Captain Lucic. They're denoted and L and B, respectively. In the middle of the conversation, Beara asked to speak to Zoka. Zoka is the nickname for Zoran Malinic, the commander of the military police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. And what I've just gotten through asking the witness about is the conversation, and you'll see that that is denoted as Z -- this part of the conversation, the collocutors are denoted as Z and B, respectively, Zoka and Beara, and you'll see that from the end of the intercept. So I think the collocutors are quite clearly denoted in the intercept. The transition point is very clear because Beara says: "Let me talk to him." And then it says: "Yes." And it's on the second page in the -- in the English, and then Zoka gets on the line. And he says: "Hi, Zoka." So it is very clear that the collocutors have changed at that point and then we have this whole conversation about 500, 200 that have gotten through, some that have gotten through that night and the fact that some of them are killing each other and that Beara says: "Excellent, let them continue." So I think it's very clear and the intercept speaks for itself. I should add also that the intercept is in evidence and that the person who took the intercept offered evidence before this -- before this Tribunal, before this Court. And if there was any question about the sequence, the collocutors, the context of the intercept, I'm certain that General Tolimir would have addressed those issues in the cross-examination of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe you are satisfied with the Prosecutor's answer, General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It does not satisfied me, because I did not receive an explanation who the participants in this part of the conversation are, when they say that they were killing each other. Is this the same conversation also recorded at 10.00, or subsequently? In any case, I don't want to affect the further course of the Prosecutor's examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I was about to say. If you so wish, you can address this again during your cross-examination. Mr. Prosecutor, I have a question for you. Regarding page 8 of the transcript. I noticed that the witness said, on line 11 through 14, on page 8 of the transcript that in his language, the intercept states that Colonel Beara purportedly said, Let them kill each other and kill themselves. There is a difference between the text in B/C/S and the text in English. Can we ask the witness to read this out so that we have a translation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Let me see if I can find the exact point in the B/C/S. It should be on page 2 of the B/C/S, and it's just above where it says Konjevic Polje, which is about, looks to me about 12 or 13 lines down. And we can start probably around line -- line 2 where it says, "Yes, yes" in the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If can you read that out, Mr. Malinic, perhaps that will --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Beara: "Yes, yes." Then Zoka or Zoran: "Because I can't." Then Beara: "Well, yes. It's a clear thing." When we have three dots, these are probably parts that were inaudible or that were not recorded, so not the entire context is in the conversation. Then Zoka: "Because here and then ... they are killing themselves. There are many wounded." And then Beara: "What? They're killing each other? Then no answer by Zoka, or, rather, there are three dots, probably not recorded. And then Beara says: "Uh-huh," which means I must have explained something. And then Zoka says: "Killing," with three dots before and after. Then Beara: "Excellent. Let them continue like that. Fuck it." Zoran: "That's it. That's how it is. That's what the situation is. I am, then three dots." Beara: "Bye then." That's the part of the conversation. Should I continue? Zoran: No answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't -- is that satisfactory, Mr. President, or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's fine, unless one of the parties would like to add something to this. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. What I'd like to show the witness is P2205. And just for the Court's information, the previous exhibit that I showed, P663, what I showed was P663B, there is also a P663A which is a handwritten or notebook version of this intercept. And the passages that the witness has just referred to are, in fact, reflected in the transcript of the handwritten intercept. So we have two different translations of two different documents reflecting exactly the same thing but the translations are somewhat different.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here we have an intercept, sir, that's recorded at 10.15 at the bottom of this page in English. And can you see here that it refers to Major Malinic, the commander of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment Armoured Battalion, and it says that he and Colonel Pero Salapura, VRS security service, are at the football field in Kasaba village. It says: "18 kilometres to the north-west of Srebrenica where they are receiving the arrested Muslims. There are around 500 prisoners there at the moment. As for the weapons, around 30 machine-guns were confiscated. General Mladic is currently in Bratunac." Were you with -- first of all, do you know who Colonel Salapura is, or was, back in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Before I answer your question, you said around ten machine-guns but the B/C/S version says around 30 machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe I said 30 and maybe the transcript doesn't reflect that. In any event, do you know who Colonel Salapura is or was back in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Salapura was at the command, or, rather, the Main Staff of the VRS. And according to my knowledge, he was discharging the duty of the security officer. He was the chief of security service, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you with him on 13 July 1995, as indicated here in the intercept?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 13, line 6, it says, "He was the chief of security service." I think that the witness said "intelligence service."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I heard in French also. Let's ask the witness to clarify. Witness, please, who was Colonel Salapura in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the information I had, Colonel Salapura was the chief of intelligence service at the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There we have it. Thank you. The Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you again, Mr. Malinic. Were you with Colonel Salapura, as is indicated here, on the football field at around 10.00 on 13 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's highly probable that Colonel Salapura was in the Nova Kasaba sector. Whether he was at the barracks or at the football field, this is something I cannot confirm with certainty. But I would pay -- point your attention to this. I cannot talk with Colonel Beara at 10.15 from my office, because I only had a telephone at my office at the school, and be, at the same time, when I'm talking with Colonel Beara at the football field, at 10.15 hours. It can be either one or the other. I could not have been in two different places at one and the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you see Colonel Salapura in and around that area? You said that the school was 300 metres away from the football field. That's not a very large distance. Did you see Colonel Salapura around 10.00 on the 13th of July 1995? And when I say "around 10.00," I don't mean 10.02 or 10.05. I mean 10.00.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It says here the 13th of July, 1995, at 1015, 924. And on the basis of this document, I'm answering to your questions. I apologise if I did something wrong. I said that there is high probability that Colonel Salapura was at Kasaba. Whether he was at the barracks or on the football field, that is something I cannot confirm with 100 per cent certainty and say, Yes, he was for sure at 10.00 in Kasaba or on the football field and that I met him and talked to him. It is highly probable that in the course of the 13th of July, he was in the Nova Kasaba sector. But at what time, I'm not sure I could say that with 100 per cent certainty, what the time was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you P105.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would just ask the Prosecutor for an explanation. As Exhibit P2205 in the Serbian version only contains one paragraph but in the English version, I have just checked in e-court, it has much more text. Could we just have an explanation for the record what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't know if Mr. Gajic is referring to the -- I think you're referring to the translation of the document that's in evidence? I believe the reason for it is because this translation applies to more than one intercept, and so you see the translation of other intercepts in addition to the intercept that's in the B/C/S. And the one that I'm drawing the witness's attention to, specifically, is the one at 10.15, as he pointed out, which corresponds to the B/C/S translation -- I mean the B/C/S transcript on the left side of the -- of the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Gajic, that -- we are all able to see this on the screen. In the English, we see an intercept at five minutes past 9.00 and another one at 10.15. In B/C/S, on the left-hand side of the screen, we can also see the conversation that took place at 10.15 and that is what we have been focussing on. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I just wanted to have this clarified for the record so that later on there wouldn't be any problems during the use of this exhibit and when presenting final arguments or for any other purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you. That's been settled. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to show the witness P105. Yeah, okay. And if I could focus just in the middle of this map. We have to go down, please. That's right where the circle is, and the arrow. Yes, please. If you can blow that area up. And it will have to be a little bit bigger, right there. And let's move the screen -- let's centre the arrow part of it a little bit more. That's it. And we'll blow up that point where you are right now, blow that up a little bit. Yeah. Okay. And if we could just see the top part of the screen a little bit better. That's -- a little bit more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what you see in front of you now, Mr. Malinic? And if you don't, that's okay. I have another map I can use.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I see that this shows the combat operations and the breakthrough from encirclement. I can judge that by the position of the blue arrow and the blue and red lines. It's an attempt of units to break through but who this is, that's something I cannot clearly read what area this is from the map because the place names are not legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will show you another map in just a moment. We have evidence in this case, as you -- as you probably can guess, that this was the direction that the column took out of Srebrenica. What I'd like to do is show you 65 ter 1463 so that we can focus on the left side of this screen where that arrow is a -- in a little more detail, which I think would be helpful to orient us all to this -- to the context of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So if I could show the witness, please, 65 ter 1463, we'll find that same area. If we could just focus now on the bottom right-hand corner where the arrow is once again. A little bit bigger. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let us know if we need to blow that up a little bit more. But, Mr. Malinic, can you now orient yourself to the area that's depicted here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is sufficient. Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At the top of the screen, you can see an area that's marked Konjevic Polje. There's an intersection there.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what roads intersect there, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the right, or to the east, the road leading from Konjevic Polje leads in the direction of Bratunac. And the road which is leading to the south from the intersection is the road which leads from Konjevic Polje in the direction of Nova Kasaba and Milici. And the road leading to the north from Konjevic Polje leads in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I may have you mark this -- in fact, I'd like you to mark this map. But can you indicate on here, if you can see first, where the football pitch is, and where the school is. Are you able to see those locations on this map? Or approximately, those locations.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Then I'd like you to mark them, please. With the help of the usher, we'll arrange for that to be done.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that the football field is this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you could mark that with number 1 for the football field next to the circle you've drawn.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you could mark the school with the number 2.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a bit more to the south. Can we erase this or ... I went a bit to the north from the school. Because I cannot really figure how this pen works and whether I can erase it. Erase this one, too, please, because we'll then see ... fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let's try again.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the football field. And number 2 is the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you indicate with the number 3 where you dispatched these five soldiers that came back with the three prisoners early in the morning on the 13th, as you've previously described.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the stream, the direction of the breakthrough, and then, later on, the biggest number of prisoners who were arrested, it was here, on this axis and in this direction. From the woods, the stream is to the right. This is the area where the first prisoners were captured and where, during the day, the biggest number of soldiers of the 38th Division surrendered themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have in the record "the 38th Division." Do you mean the 28th Division? That's number one.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 28th, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The second is, could you indicate or mark the line that you've drawn here showing the axis of where those soldiers were sent with number 3, so that we have it in the record.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The red line which I last drew shows the direction in which the Muslim forces from the 28th Division were moving. There was a path that was several metres wide because they probably went in a column, several of them moving abreast, and this is the direction that they were moving in, towards Radanj and further on in the direction of Cerska. And the line of blockade, because you asked me where the group was sent, and to show where the first three, or, rather, the first five were went, was that you in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I just want you to mark the map with a number 3 where they were sent.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were sent to this line, which I just marked. They left the barracks. Whether they went along the road, that's something I cannot tell you. Or perhaps they went along the Jadar river which flows below the school. From this point in time, I cannot say any more which road they took to reach the place, where the units of the 28th Division were crossing the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you saying you're not able to mark it, or -- all I want you to do is put number 3 on the map where it was that you told them to go. That's all.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was a misunderstanding, I'm sorry. I thought you wanted me to mark the path along which they moved. This is why I said I'm not sure whether they took the Jadar river valley or whether they took the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this marked exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The map as annotated by the witness is admitted, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map marked by the witness under 65 ter document 1463 shall be assigned Exhibit P2275. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked a question by Presiding Judge earlier in your testimony about the direction or what road it was that these -- that the column took. You said that they crossed a road. And the Presiding Judge asked you what road they had crossed. Can you tell us on this map which road you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the road from Konjevic Polje to Nova Kasaba, which is marked with a red line. Should I mark it in any way or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. That would be helpful, actually.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now it's blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It will be helpful if you mark the area on the road that they crossed. That would be, I think, more useful. So you don't have to mark the whole road but just mark the spot or the area on the road that they crossed.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you could place a number 1 next to that, that would be helpful as well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this marked exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is admitted. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 1463 marked by the witness in court for the second time shall be assigned Exhibit P2276. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to show the witness P857 -- I'm sorry, P858.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what we have on the screen in front of you now, Mr. Malinic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a shot of the stadium or, rather, the football in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the middle of the field, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the middle of the field are the prisoners from the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what -- and that's a square shape, is it, that we can see in the picture? Or a rectangle?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it looks more like a rectangle than a square.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then we can see a long rectangle, almost a line, to the left of that square, or those prisoners, in the photograph. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, these were the people from Milici and the surrounding area who had come to see the soldiers who were now POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is it your recollection that these people that came to see the soldiers were lined up? Because they appear to be lined up in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one lined them up. They probably sat down like that themselves so that they could see and possibly recognise some of the persons who were among the prisoners. That is my assumption. I know that there were quite a few of them. I'm not sure what the number was, but there were many who had come to see who were the imprisoned soldiers. Because many of them knew people from the area. Perhaps they worked in the same places before the war, because the majority of them worked at the mine in Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you exclude the possibility that the people that are lined up in a long rectangle on the left that you believe are civilians or bystanders from Milici? Is it possible that those are also prisoners? Do you exclude that possibility?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I would exclude that possibility. The prisoners were brought to the pitch from the eastern side, looking at the map. I don't see any logic in why they would be in -- lined up in this western part. This is an possibility that these were people who were still supposed to be registered and identified, since the location where they were registered was -- I'm sorry, I touched the screen again. The place where they were registered was among the trees. We can't see it here. That's why I say that there is a possibility that this line of people may also be prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you P857. And here we have a slightly larger perspective of this area. And what I want to focus you on, if I can, and perhaps have you mark it, is the following: Were the prisoners, first of all, secured by your unit at the football field?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My unit was in the area between the hill, just behind the school, and down to the stream I marked on the first map, where the main point of breakthrough of the division forces was. That was the area secured by my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in securing the football field, approximately where were your men positioned, inside the pitch and along its perimeter? Can you give us an indication of where they would have been, or, were, rather.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I had very few soldiers at my disposal, I used a minimum number of them, which could still provide efficient security for the unit. That security detail was on the side. Perhaps we can zoom in on the left upper corner. Perhaps we could see where a white vehicle was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to see the vehicle that you were talking about on this -- in this frame?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the vehicle. But I can't tell whether it's a BVP, that is to say, a combat vehicle of the military police with a mounted machine-gun. In any case, it was supposed to cover this area of the field. It could engage any part of the field without putting any of my soldiers in danger. On the other hand, if we look at the road next to the woods, there were also a few soldiers there who provided security. That is how I used a minimum of forces to cover the entire field area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's mark this photo then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe we can zoom out a little bit so that we can mark both areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, can you find the area where you had the BVP vehicle and mark that with a number 1.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure that this is the combat vehicle, but, in any case, it was located in this corner. And the few soldiers I mentioned were in this area, just in front of the prisoners. Do you want me to mark that location with 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. And those indicate these three dots. How many soldiers did you have there, by the way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's deleted now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. We'll try it again, I think. Okay. Thank you. How many soldiers did you have in the area that you've marked number 2, if you could just tell us for the record?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At location number 2, I can't tell you precisely how many, but three to five, at the most. And next to the APC, there was a member of the crew who manned the machine-gun, and probably the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were there -- oh, there's one other thing I'd like you to do. Could you mark the direction of Konjevic Polje with an arrow; the direction of Milici with the other arrow. Of the road.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you put the letter M for Milici; and K/P for Konjevic Polje, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Other than the men that you had in position number 2 and position number 1, did you have any other men in the area securing the football stadium, or the prisoners, from the other sides; that is, the side where the stream is, or the river, to the north, or to the south.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had those soldiers who were part of the blockade line, who were facing the members of the division arriving from the hills. They were deployed along the line that was there to prevent the breakthrough of the 28th Division forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, what I'm referring to specifically is the stadium itself, or the pitch. You've indicated position 1 and 2, and I want to know if there's any -- if there were any other soldiers in that immediate vicinity securing the field itself and the prisoners inside it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not part of the security, but in this corner, facing Konjevic Polje, which is closer to the arrow marked with K/P, this is where the medical station was set up to administer first aid, if needed. It was manned by medical personnel, and, as such, they were not part of the security detail that was there to guard the prisoners. As for the part where I placed the number 2, marking the group of soldiers, there was a table with one officer and one soldier who were registering the prisoners. Every prisoner had to come up to the table with his or her ID, and then they were included in the list of those captured by the officer. Now, whether there were any other soldiers next to the table keeping order, that is something I can't say with any precision. I can't say whether there was one or two or no one, primarily because we were able to control the prisoners from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you could just mark the exhibit with the number 3 where you've indicated the medical personnel were.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this marked exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Mr. Vanderpuye. Just before that, I would like to ask a clarification, a question. Witness, on page 26 of the transcript, line 9, you said that prisoners had IDs on them and they were showing them to an officer and a soldier. Were you able to see that ID, or at least a few of these IDs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was. I wasn't there throughout the period at the stadium, but when I was, I could see the following: Anyone who had any identity document or something that could identify them, handed those over so that their particulars could be entered in the list that was drawn up by the officer. Those who did not have any documents on them simply stated their first and last name and basic information, and a remark was made that they did not have any ID and were thus not identified by documents. In other words, not all those who were captured had such documents which could confirm their identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Now, based on those ID documents, was it possible to see if they were civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was impossible to see whether someone was a civilian or a soldier based on an ID alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Registrar, the Prosecutor requested to tender document -- the document as marked by the witness. So it will be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, very well, to be very clear, Mr. Registrar, the document will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter document -- apologies, Your Honours. Exhibit P857, marked in court by the witness, shall be assigned Exhibit P2277. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we still have it up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And just before we go to the break, I wanted to ask you, Mr. Malinic, to the bottom of the right of the screen, or the right corner of the screen, I should say, we can see some vehicles down there which appear to be buses. If we zoom out a little bit, we can see some more on the road. Does that comport with your recollection of the events on 13 July at around that time, around 2.00, 1400 hours?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose those were the buses transporting civilians from Srebrenica to Kladanj. I don't know if it happened at 2.00 exactly because they were transporting them throughout the day. I don't know what time of day it was exactly. We didn't pay much attention to it, as we did not believe it was an important piece of information to have, to know exactly at what time a bus passed by. In any case, it is clear that there were civilians on board those buses who were being transported from Srebrenica to Kladanj. They were escorted by the officers and soldiers of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now is a good time to break, Mr. President. I think it's the break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Indeed, we shall take a break until 11.00. The session is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Mr. Vanderpuye, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Malinic, just before we broke, you mentioned that there were civilians on board the buses that we could see in the photograph. I think that is P857. And that these buses were being escorted by officers and soldiers of UNPROFOR. You are aware, of course, that that wasn't continuous, those escorts weren't continuous, throughout the 13th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of the fact that those escorts did not continue throughout the 13th of July. On the buses, passing by the stadium, I believe there were also UNPROFOR officers and soldiers in each and every bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You remember being approached by a DutchBat officer by the name of Egbers that day who reported to you that he and his colleagues had been stopped along the road and divested of their equipment, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Egbers arrived with three or four vehicles in the battalion barracks, asking to see an officer to discusses some problems he had encountered during that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mm-hm. And those problems related to equipment being taken from UNPROFOR officers and their inability to escort the buses; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The equipment that was taken from them -- well, I can't recall exactly what equipment it was. But he asked that we draw up a list of all that equipment. We did that, and the copy of the list was given to Lieutenant Egbers. The other copy remained in the MP battalion. I promised to inform my superiors with -- or about the incident and that we will do our utmost to have the equipment returned to them. That is why Lieutenant Egbers was a given a copy of the list of equipment. I can't recall what equipment specifically it was. I do remember, though, that they arrived in three or four Mercedes vehicles in the barracks, that they had their weapons with them, and that they bore the insignia, the white insignia of the UN. He said that the equipment that was taken away --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the equipment that was taken was taken from his group or the group that was at the observation point. In any case, if that document is still in existence, we could see what equipment it was and if it in any way affected their ability to escort the convoys with civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How long did they stay at the barracks, Mr. Malinic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Egbers stayed in the barracks with his soldiers two or three days. During their stay, in addition to the list of equipment he provided, he asked that I secure escort for him to Potocari, where the UNPROFOR command was, or the command of his unit. During their stay in the barracks, the weapons were kept by the UNPROFOR soldiers. They also had communication means, probably by satellite. I know that because during that period of time, Lieutenant Egbers was able to communicate with his base in Split, according to the information he provided to me. When he received an approval from his command, although I don't know if it was the command in Split or the one in Potocari, that he may leave, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How did he leave, and his men, Mr. Malinic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He and the group he headed went on board a military police APC. They were taken as far as Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what happened to the Mercedes vehicles that they arrived in, Mr. Malinic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Mercedes vehicles remained in the barracks. Lieutenant Egbers received a certificate stating that the vehicles were to stay in the barracks. The reason for that was their security. It was his request that I should escort him with my soldiers to Potocari. However, due to the fact that there was still combat, I was unable to secure an escort for him who could guarantee safety to him and his people, so as to prevent any harm coming to them en route to Potocari. In the part where we were and further afield to Konjevic Polje, which is to my left, there was combat. Under such circumstances, I could not guarantee their safety. I could not guarantee that fire would not be opened --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I asked you what happened to the Mercedes. And I think you've answered that. I'm running out of time so I'm going to try to be as specific as I can with my questions, and it would be helpful if you could be specific with your answers, too. Were you aware that Egbers was stopped at gun point before he came to your barracks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you contact your superior, in relation to the complaints that Egbers gave you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who did you contact?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed my superior at the command of the Protection Regiment, and that was Lieutenant-Colonel Jovo Jazic. He probably relayed this information to the Main Staff command and informed them that at the barracks in Nova Kasaba there was a group of UNPROFOR members.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did Colonel Beara come in response to this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for issues relating the presence of Colonel Beara, there are various views and opinions. According to what I remember, I'm not 100 per cent sure that Colonel Beara was present at the barracks, but it is highly probable that he was; in particular, considering the situation that the unit was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you P526.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document should not be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is an intercept, sir, that's from the 13th of July, 1995. You can see the time indicated here as 1445 hours and it's between two individual who are not named. 1, and 2, they are designated respectively. I'd like to show you, or, first, we can see just generally it talks about the area of Konjevic Polje. We can see that at about the fifth entry or sixth entry in the intercept itself. And it talks about buses: "The column is on both sides and those buses have stopped in Zvornik. They can't pass." And then we can see the conversation continues, and 1 described that: "It is a madhouse. Some of them want to surrender, some won't." And then: "There is shooting among them and our guys are capturing them." Does this fairly reflect your recollection of what was going on in the area that you indicated on the map, in Konjevic Polje and Nova Kasaba and so on, at about that time, on that date?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was crowded. There was a lot of combat, a lot of shooting, many explosions; also members of the 28th Division who surrendered themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's go to page 2 in the English, and the bottom of this page in the B/C/S. And we can see here an entry that refers to you. It says: "This Malinic down there, he called Major Savcic. He says he does not know how long this commotion here is going to last and it's not possible to get through. And here ... up there, I have," and it appears to be a radio set, "when they said two buses, then they also ordered four trucks." With respect to the reference to you having called Major Savcic, is that accurate? Does it reflect your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who Major Savic is. I do not know him or I cannot recollect now who Major Savic would be. In the unit and at the commend of the 65th Regiment, there was no Major Savic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you call Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic? Savcic, not Savic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday during the examination, I said that I did not know where Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic was, and I did not have his number. From this point in time, I cannot recollect whether I called Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic and talked to him at the time indicated here. There is a possibility that we talked on the phone several times during the day, but whether it was at this time, I cannot tell you with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And let me just ask this one other question: As part of the military police battalion, did you have a communications company, a communications unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the establishment, there was a communications detachment which was a part of the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said "according to the establishment." What I would like to know is: In fact, was there one there, or one that was operating in the area of Nova Kasaba, or communications personnel in the area of Nova Kasaba, on 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I said that according to the establishment, we had a communications squad. This squad was operational and it was part of the military police battalion. In the Kasaba sector, we had a code, and we also had a radio relay piece of equipment which was used for communication with the command of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The unit is a squad rather than a detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in order to reach the command of the regiment or other units, you would have gone through or used the communications squad that was available to the battalion command; yes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications squad had a primary task of taking care of the radio relay piece of equipment which was outside of the school complex. It was positioned on a hill above the school, and it had to meet certain technical criteria. The place where it was had to have certain technical characteristics so that communication could be established. In the process of establishing communication with the command of the 65th Protection Regiment, communications soldiers were not necessary. You would simply dial the number on a telephone set and you would reach the person you wanted to talk to at the regiment command. Also, the squad, that is to say, one or two soldiers, were in charge of the code. They were specially trained soldiers who had to meet certain security criteria to be allowed to work on the code because that was a key that they were handling.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you P125. Oh, wait a minute. Let me show you P411. B. P441B.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is a confidential exhibit and should not be broadcast. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: 411B, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is another intercept which I'm sure you've seen before. It's timed at 1405 hours. And it's 13 July 1995 also. And it refers to the football pitch. And then it says: "Brother, don't take anyone. I'll send you an urgent telegram now. Don't take anyone" --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I can't see that. I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I think we've got it now and it starts at the bottom of the page. Do you see it now? It's at the very bottom of the screen and you'll see the frequency of 254.300, and then it says "pravac ji jugoistok." Can you see it now, Mr. Malinic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this intercept, you can see, is timed at 1405 hours between X and Y; they're unknown. And X says: "Where is that?" Y says: "Here at the football pitch." And X says: "Is it visible?" Y says: "It is." X says: "Brother, don't take anyone. I'll send you an urgent telegram now. Don't take anyone." And it says: "Put out of sight. Maybe." And then it says: "I'll end you the telegram now and explain it to you." Y says: "Go ahead." And X says: "Secure it well and you'll get it now in the telegram." First of all, do you know what this is about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This telegram, or, rather, this conversation, is something that is presented to me for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You sure about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. When you were interviewed back in December of 2005, I believe you were shown this particular telegram. And it's on page 16 of the English. If you want, I will put the B/C/S up for you. But let me just read what it says. It says in the question: "Okay. Now it's very clear that the two people speaking on this intercept are talking about the soccer field, and one person is saying, 'Do not accept any more. I'll send you a telegram and explain.' And shortly after this, we know that the telegram was sent, in fact, I have the original with me. But before we get on to that, do you recall this conversation? Did you take part in it?" And your answer was: "I really can't tell you anything about it." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. For the record, it's transcript page 16, line 18 -- rather, line 12 through 17 in the -- 12 through 18, I'm sorry, in the English; and page 14, line 31, through page 15, line 32 in the B/C/S. I can put it up on the screen. But I don't think it's necessary at this point. Let me show you P125. This is a document, Mr. Malinic, that I'm quite sure that you've seen before. You can see this one is timed at 1400 hours, which is close in time --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Which is close in time to the intercept I just showed you. And it states -- well, first of all, the title says it is IKM forward command post of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment at Borike. And it says that it is to the commander of the Main Staff, to the assistant commander for morale, religious, legal affairs of the Main Staff, and to the commander of the military police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. That would be you, yes? At least by title. And it is entitled: "Procedure for treatment of prisoner of war" and recounts that there are over a thousand members of the -- former 28th Division of the so-called BH Army captured in the area of Dusanovo and then it says "(Kasaba)." Is that the area in which your units were situated on 13 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you can see here at the very bottom of the screen, it says, "Delivered, 1510 hours, 13 July 1995." And type-signed by Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic. Were you shown this document before?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was shown this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask Mr. Vanderpuye to say where the signature of Mr. Savcic can you found on this document, because he said that there was a facsimile of the signature. I don't see it and I wish to see it. So can that be noted, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, this appears to be a translation issue. What I said was it is typed-signed. It is a typewritten name of "pukovnik," Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic. It says Komandant, on top of it, and I think you can probably see it on the screen in front of you. That's what I referred to when I said "type-signed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is quite clear that the document was typed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is, however, signed on the left-hand side of the document, and I believe the Trial Chamber has received the evidence concerning the signature of the individual who -- well, of that individual and the circumstances relating to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Malinic, can you tell us about this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we just zoom in a little bit more so that I can read it once again, if that's all right. I have read it. I can say the following about this document: I can see that it was addressed to the commander of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army for his information, then to the assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs of the Main Staff of VRS for his information, and the commander of the military police battalion, "order." So this document is an order for me. It says at the beginning that there are more than 1.000 prisoners, members of the 28th Division. Assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the Main Staff of the VRS proposes the following measures. I think that if you look at one and the other structure, it cannot be an order, and the assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the Main Staff proposes the following measures. If it's an order, it just states what needs to be done. In my opinion, the assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the Main Staff of the VRS can propose measures to the Main Staff commander, rather than to Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic. Primarily because the assistant commander can give advice and can say what he would do, but in a document which is entitled as an order, he cannot say that the assistant commander for security and intelligence proposes the following measures. I cannot see from this whether this is an order for me to do that or if it's a proposal. If I look at it as a superior officer, if we then have a look at the categories: "Prohibit access to all unauthorised individuals filming and photographing of prisoners." I could do that. Number 2: "Prohibit traffic for all United Nations vehicles en route Zvornik, Vlasenica until further notice. Re-route them via Zvornik, Sekovici, Vlasenica and back." I could not do that. Because if Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic sent this telegram, he knew where I was and that I could not close down this road because Zvornik is mentioned here. So with a part of my unit, I was supposed to be stationed in Zvornik in order to be able to carry out this order. Number 3: "Commander of the military police battalion shall take measures to remove war prisoners from the main Milici-Zvornik road. Place them somewhere indoors or in an area protected from observation from the ground or the air." If this is an order that I received, then, as a subordinate officer, I would have to act in accordance with the order. All prisoners who were at the stadium at 1400 hours remained there until their departure; that is to say, until the arrival of vehicles and their transport. If I had received this order and had not carried it out, then a criminal report should have been filed against me because I had not carried out the orders of my superior. And, finally, the commander --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once the commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you talk a little bit slowly, please, so that the interpreters could interpret precisely what you are saying and that this can be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Do I need to repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think we've gotten what you've said so far. But you just need to slow down so that the interpreters can have a chance to interpret what you say to those of us who don't speak your language. Let me ask you this question, Mr. Malinic: You're saying that if you had received this order, then you would -- you did not discharge it. Is that the gist of it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I say that if I had received it, I would have had to carry it out, or else my superior would have filed a criminal report against me, asking why I had not carried out the order. As I explained that the prisoners had remained at the football field until their arrival of buses and their transport, I either did not act in accordance with this order or never received this telegram. I am an officer who esteems and honours my superiors. At least I was like that. I carried out orders. It is impossible that I received this telegram and did not carry out the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you saying that the order is not legitimate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not saying that the order is not legitimate. I read it from the beginning, and it is my conclusion that either things were not done properly or the document was not drafted properly, but it was not in keeping with standard practice of publishing or issuing orders. If you look at the format of the telegram itself, any educated officer who has ever issued a single order would tell you that an order may not look like this and not in this form. That's what I'm trying to say. I won't discuss whether the signature of the commander is there or not. You can all see that it is not there. I will not try to dispute that fact. There's another thing. The fourth point which I did not complete where it says that the battalion commander, upon receiving this order, will get in touch with General Miletic and acquire additional explanations and seek verification of whether what was proposed by the commander of the Main Staff was correct. In other words, this order should have been approved by the commander of the Main Staff. It turns out that this document did not have the force of an order until it was approved. In other words, these were just proposed measures. In an order for implementation needs to be approved by the commander of the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you contact General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all likelihood, during the 13th, I did speak to General Miletic. It seems he was the only general in the Main Staff command post. And the other officers from the Main Staff Command, starting with the commander, as well as the Chief of Staff, were outside the area of the command post. They were somewhere in the field. We probably spoke. If you're trying to ask me whether we discussed this or something else, such as General Miletic inquiring about the situation in Nova Kasaba, then I'd say that there's a high probability that we did talk. I don't know, though, why I, as the MP battalion commander, would need to get in touch with General Miletic by communication means when, at the command post of the 65th Protection Regiment, was -- that command post was 2- to 300 metres from the command post of the Main Staff, and Jovo Jazic was there, who was the Chief of Staff of the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Malinic. I don't want to belabour the point, and I guess I should put this up. It is 65 ter 2781, which is your statement. And we'll have to go to page 19 in the English and page 18, I believe, in the B/C/S. While that's coming up, do you recall being asked about whether you thought this particular document, that is, P125, was legitimate or authentic? Do you remember being asked that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in 2005, when I provided the statement in the office? Then, yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At line 21 through 28 in the English, and 18 through 26, I believe, in the B/C/S, you were asked, first, does this, the document, in question: "Does it look legitimate, authentic to you?" That was the question. And your answer is: "If it was sent by the forward command post, I don't know why it would be in any other archive," because the investigator told you it was recovered from the Drina Corps archive. "If it is an original, I say it again, it has to be signed. It has to be a stamp on the copy that arrives through code. There is no stamp and signature on that copy. On the original, it has to be signed and stamped. Every order has to contain information as to who drafted it, who typed it. It we do this by initials. On this document, I don't see it, so I can't tell you what the status of this document is. One can conclude for what I have [sic] just said, no, it's not." Meaning, no, it's not legitimate or authentic. Is that what you're saying here today, or are you saying something different?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today, I analysed the document in all its parts. I believe we came to the conclusion that it is not an order but, actually, a proposal that needed to be approved by the commander of the Main Staff. I read it carefully today. I don't know how much attention I paid to those details when I provided my statement to the ICTY office in Belgrade. At that time, I probably focussed more on the elements necessary for a document to be an order. I tried to approach it from this technical standpoint, and, now, I focussed on that part of the order which includes the addressee and whether it was a full-fledged order or a proposal. There's another thing I stressed, which is it should be in the archives of the regiment and not in the archives of the Drina Corps, because it is not stated anywhere that this message or this document was to be sent to the command of the Drina Corps. So one needs to ask one's self how this would ended up in a place where it was not to be sent in the first place. I, as an officer, do not understand that. Maybe somebody picked it up from a unit, and we can see that it was addressed to the commander of the Main Staff, assistant commander for morale and religious affairs, and to the MP battalion commander of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment. If there were four addressees on the list and yet it surfaced at a fifth location, then we have a problem: Is this a valid document or not? That is why I raised that issue in 2005, in all likelihood.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In fact, in 2005, you discussed a number of the provisions in the document, of the items that are listed 1 through 4, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the item -- in the exhibit, rather, there are a number of items that are listed. You went through a couple of them just a few moments ago; items 1 through 4. You discussed those during the course of your interview as well, in 2005; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible. It is possible that I discussed the points in 2005. I didn't look at the whole text. You directed me to the part where I discussed the technical characteristics. I didn't look into what I said then, if I talked about the various items of the order at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You did read your statement before you started testifying here; yes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I read it in your office on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss this document with Milomir Savcic? That is, either before your interview or after your interview.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the past ten years, I seldom met Lieutenant-Colonel Savcic. I don't know if we discussed this. Actually, I cannot see -- say with 100 per cent certainty whether we discussed this document or not. I can't be certain either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned in the last ten years. Let me ask you maybe this way: In the last ten years, had you discussed this document with Mr. Savcic, what would be the reason for that? Why would you have discussed this document with Mr. Savcic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a hypothetical question. Why would I discuss it? And my answer is hypothetical. I don't know if I did or did not. If I did, hypothetically if I did, it was probably because something surrounding this document was discussed during his interview with the Prosecution. Now whether I was able to assist in any way in this, that is something I don't know. I don't see any reason or the sense of this order. I don't know why it is so important. Maybe my perception is too narrow, but I don't see anything in this order that would be wrong. In this proposal/order, I don't see anything that has to do with the time and area of combat operations that be would wrong. All armed forces in the world work the same way. There was one illogical thing which struck me at the time, and that was that the road in the area of combat operations not be cut off or have it sealed. It was illogical to have people recording videotaping POWs --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just asked you whether or not you discussed it with Mr. Savcic. If your answer is you don't remember, you might have, could have, or would have, that's all I want to know. Are you saying that you don't recall discussing this document with Mr. Savcic in the last, say, ten years?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already that I don't remember discussing this document with Colonel Savcic in the past ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You indicated on -- just a moment. When I showed you P857 - I believe that was the aerial image of Nova Kasaba football field with prisoners on it - you indicated that a column of individuals that we can see on that photograph might have been lined up to provide identification. Did you make lists of these prisoners that were in the custody of your unit on the football field at that time, on the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A list was drawn up. Perhaps not of all the prisoners, but at least 90 per cent or 95 per cent of them. There was a list of those who were captured and placed in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And why wasn't that list completed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain whether the percentage was 90, or 100, or 98. If there is a possibility that the list is incomplete, one reason for it could be that the buses used to transport those captured soldiers arrived before the prisoner list was completed. I mentioned that as a possibility, not as my knowledge or 100 per cent truth. Maybe all of the prisoners were listed, although I'm not sure. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you -- yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
