utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, as it is midday now, past midday, you have used up almost three hours and 45 minutes, if I'm not mistaken. Maybe Mr. -- the Registrar might have more precise information. I do not want to put you under pressure, but I believe that it is time for you to complete your examination-in-chief because you required three hours. So please finish earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm doing my best, and I'm trying to ask very specific, directed questions, and I'm hoping to persuade the witness to give me very specific and directed answers, and I think that may help to speed things up. I have, essentially, two areas that I'd like to cover with this witness, and I'm hoping that they will be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that you had been involved in making list of these prisoners. You said 90 per cent, and then you said that it could be 100 per cent and you're not sure. Do you have any recollection of the process of listing the prisoners being interrupted at any point?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The process, or the order, I didn't personally participate in the listing of prisoners, but I did order that all prisoners should be listed. The rules of service of the military police regulates that all those brought into custody need to be identified by best means available. By the same token, my order was in keeping with the rules of the military police, which is that all prisoners should be listed. Now, whether the process of listing those prisoners was completed -- well, it began a few hours following the capture of the first group, and it went on until the soldiers were put on the buses; the prisoners, that is. I cannot say with any certainty whether they were all listed because their bringing in was not completed by 6.00 p.m. In between 6.00 p.m. and the time the prisoners boarded the buses, there may still have been some of them coming in. In other words, the process was not completed at a certain point in time. The process of capturing soldiers lasted up to the moment when they -- they began boarding the buses. I don't know whether they were all listed. I don't even know whether the process was interrupted at any point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Malinic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's all I want to know. If you know it's interrupted, can you tell us, and if you don't know, you can tell us that, too. I think it will save some time if you can respond directly to my question. Did you tell Colonel Keserovic -- you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We could say that the process was interrupted when the commander of the Main Staff arrived in the area of the football field and when the commander of the Main Staff, General Ratko Mladic, addressed the prisoners. Prior to his arrival, I was not at the stadium, at the field. When General Mladic arrived, I was informed by way of radio that he had arrived and I went there. I arrived a few minutes later. Now whether the process was interrupted, yes, during the time he was addressing the prisoners who were in the field at Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you tell General, or, rather, Colonel Keserovic - then - on or around the 16th or 17th of July that the process was interrupted when General Mladic said that there was no need to make lists because the prisoners would be going home?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having said that to General Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you saying you don't remember specifically saying that to General Keserovic, or you don't remember what you said to General Keserovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what I said to General Keserovic, because it was 16 years ago, and I don't remember how the conversation went. I only know that General Keserovic came with the task of unifying the activities of those units in the area of Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, Bratunac in order to have a search of terrain conducted. He came there with an intention to unify the -- unify or co-ordinate the activities of those units who were in that part of the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were your units among those involved in the action, which General Keserovic came to, as you say, unify? The activities that you referred to just a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat operation of terrain search is one of the most complex ones. My unit was along the same blockade line that had been set up on the 13th of July, 1995. Its task was to remain there until the search of terrain was completed. The principal forces used to search the terrain had to include the Bratunac Brigade and perhaps some other unit, but I don't know. The terrain search, in my view and my conclusion which is what I informed the superior command, was that it was not completed. It was simply stated that the terrain search was completed after a certain period of time, but I don't know whether it was one, two, or three days later. As for General Keserovic's stay in the area of my battalion, as far as I recall, was a very short one. I think he spent most of his time focussing on the Bratunac Brigade, which was supposed to carry out the search; while the other units involved were deployed along the blockade line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And yours was one of those units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit was part of the blockade line, at the same location at which it had been since the 13th of July, 1995. No other special task was received by us, in terms of the terrain search. We remained where we were. In military parlance, there were those units who were part of the blockade and those units searching the terrain. As far as I know, that unit was supposed to have been the Bratunac Brigade. I don't know whether any other units participated in it. General Keserovic, who, at the time was a lieutenant-colonel, was supposed to co-ordinate the work of all those units that were in the field at that time; that is to say, starting with the blockade line and up to the units executing the search.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Malinic, do you know whether prisoners were captured as a result of those -- or that search of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether anyone was captured during the search of the terrain, because, as far as I know, this was taking place from the 16th or the 17th until about the 20th, because in such an extensive area it cannot be completed in just one day. I don't know whether anyone was taken prisoner during the search of the terrain. I noted that it is my opinion that the search of the terrain was not even carried out as it should be done. The units which were doing the search of the terrain were supposed to come and link up with units which were engaged on the blockade. When that is done, then such a search of the terrain is completed. However, as this link-up of the units which were in charge of searching the terrain did not link up with units who were in charge of the blockade, and I primarily mean my own unit when I say that, my personal opinion is that the search of the terrain was never completely done. Whether anyone was taken prisoner during the process or not, this is something I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, that's my question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tell you, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a question and try to answer the question. Don't save it for last. Try to answer it first. Are you aware of the fact that this Trial Chamber has evidence before it that as many as 200 prisoners were captured, and some children were captured, during the sweep of this terrain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The witness already answered that he does not know this. I would ask Mr. Vanderpuye not to ask questions that are leading the witness which include something that he knows but just ask them in such a way that the witness should only state what he knows or does not know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you heard that as many as 200 prisoners were captured, including some children during the course of the sweep of the terrain? Have you heard that before coming here to testify today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I hear that during the search of the terrain anyone was taken prisoner. I noted that no one from the Bratunac Brigade or any other unit which participated in the search of the terrain did not come out to the blockade line where my unit was positioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the Court's reference, I'm referring to the testimony of PW-052, a 92 bis witness. And specifically pages 8702 through 8703 of the Popovic trial transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you very briefly, Mr. Malinic: During the period of time that your units were securing the prisoners at Nova Kasaba stadium, were you aware of, or did you hear about, any abuses of the prisoners? And, in particular, did you hear that one of the prisoners was shot and killed there at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the abuse of prisoners, there was none of that, as far as I know. They were brought to the football field where they had to sit. They were given water, and food was ordered for them through the president of the Milici municipality. I think it was primary bread because they supplied us with that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as for killings, the killing of one prisoner, this is something I heard of. And it did happen at the stadium when the prisoner attacked a soldier who was a member of the military police battalion. That was the only instance when someone lost his life, but it wasn't at anyone's whim. It was a question of self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would just, for the record, refer the Trial Chamber to the evidence of PW-16, and, in particular, I think that is admitted in this case as P1762, transcript reference 3024 through 3025.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this, Mr. Malinic, so we can conclude. Are you aware of graves, mass graves, in the area of Nova Kasaba between where your unit was stationed and the intersection that were exhumed, containing the bodies of several prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Malinic. I have no further questions for you on direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, very much, Mr. President. I appreciate your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. Thank you for finishing your examination-in-chief. We still have ten minutes before the break, so I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir if he wishes to start his cross-examination at this point. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can start, or perhaps it would be best to take the break now and then finish everything as part of one session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vanderpuye, I believe that this is a good idea. Mr. Tolimir's proposal is convenient, isn't it? Right. So we will now take a 30-minute break. We shall reconvene at 12.50. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in session. Witness, you will now be cross-examined by the accused, General Tolimir. He will be the one asking you questions. I'm absolutely certain that you will answer calmly and courteously, as you did when the Prosecutor put his questions to you. So he has the right to put questions to you, according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. General Tolimir, you have the floor. But before that, I believe you said that you needed three hours, if I'm not mistaken. So please try to do what you can; try to do your best. I don't want to put any undue pressure on you. I did not put too much pressure on the Prosecutor either. So thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I know that we will not finish today, I don't expect that we will. I did want to alert the Court that our next witness will not be ready in any event to proceed until Wednesday, so I just wanted to let you know that so it is not a surprise come Tuesday, depending on when General Tolimir completes his cross-examination and if there's any re-direct examination, that there may be a small gap between that and the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vanderpuye, I understood what you said, and I don't know how much General Tolimir will need for his examination or cross-examination, but I imagine that if he needs the same amount of time you used, we would have to -- we won't finish today so we would have to continue on Tuesday, because Monday is a day off, it's a United Nations holiday. I believe you are right, because you are saying yes, nodding. So if we do not finish today, Mr. Witness, Mr. Zoran Malinic, you will have to stay with us here in The Hague and until next Tuesday. You are a very important witness. You saw that the Prosecutor went over the time that was given to him. I imagine that you understand that. So, Mr. Prosecutor, I imagine that Witness PW-057 won't be able to come before Wednesday. Is that what you said? If we do not finish on Tuesday with the witness that we have here today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes and no. It is correct that the witness won't be ready until Wednesday. But that's independent of when this -- the current witness finishes. If he finished for example, early on Tuesday, then I expect there will be a gap, unfortunately, until the next witness. That what I was trying to express. Obviously if the current witness is not completed on Tuesday, then we'll just start later with the next witness, on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does the Defence wish to add any comment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask us to move on to cross-examination of this witness. Perhaps we might finish today, if he provides short answers, so he wouldn't have to wait until Wednesday here, because he has other things to do. So if you allow me, I would try to do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, General. I thank you for your efficiency and I hope that it will -- you will be efficient, as you said. So you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Once again, may there be peace to this house. I greet everyone present and I hope that this day of trial and the entire proceedings may finish as God wishes and not as I wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, as we speak the language, please have a look at the screen and do not start speaking before the cursor stops. And please also try to answer briefly to my questions. Thank you. Mr. Malinic, my first question is this: Who did you hand over the war prisoners from the football field to and who transported them and where, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon, or, rather, in the evening on the 13th of July, buses came along to the football field. The prisoners, the soldiers, boarded the buses, and, from what I learned later, the buses then went to Bratunac. Whether someone who was the leader of the convoy and who brought the buses, I cannot say with certainty whether that was the person who received the prisoners and took them on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the afternoon, on the 13th, was there a TV crew present, and did it do some filming of the prisoners and the activities at the football field, as you said during examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received an order from Lieutenant-Colonel Jazic on the 13th, saying that TV crews which will film the prisoners would come to the sector of Nova Kasaba in the sector of the football field and that it was not necessary to do any checks of these TV crews, because the filming of POWs and the whole situation in the Nova Kasaba area had been approved by the Main Staff. I think that there were three crews and that someone from the press centre of the VRS was leading the group which came to film the soldiers. During the filming of the POWs, they had complete freedom. They could talk to the prisoners, interview them, shoot all the details at the stadium so that, as the battalion commander, or, rather, the commander of the part of the unit that was present there at the time, I was unable to prevent or block or guide the TV crews in any way so that they would film anything according to my scenario rather than their own. They had complete freedom, in other words. I'm not sure whether the TV crews were there at the time moment when the Main Staff commander came to the football field in Nova Kasaba. It's highly probable that they were, and that they also filmed General Mladic's address to the prisoners, but I cannot say this with 100 percent certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As for your soldiers who watched the news on TV that evening, could you hear from them whether the football field in Nova Kasaba was on the news and whether everyone was informed, both the local and the international public, that the prisoners from Nova Kasaba and the football field would be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no TV signal received in Nova Kasaba. So that to your question whether the soldiers watched the TV, I cannot answer in the affirmative. The entire unit was on the positions. So even if we had been receiving the signal and had the TV programme, they could not have watched it because they were engaged in carrying out combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can it be supposed that if filming was allowed on the 13th, and if Jazic announced it to you on the 13th, if you allowed it to be done on the 13th, did these journalists who were filming that keep the information for themselves or did they inform the public about it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, I am not aware of what the further activities of the journalists and TV crews were after they had filmed what they did. Therefore, I cannot tell you anything about their further activities and whether it was broadcast, whether it was published in the media, or any other information about that. I could not learn anything about that, or watch that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As you were informed that you should allow the media representatives in, and as they were there and as they freely talked to the prisoners, as you told us, tell us, whether the POWs were registered at the time? Were lists of them being made? And could the media representatives and the POWs communicate freely?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the visit of the TV crews to the football field, the POWs were being listed and the TV crews had the right to talk to them and film all the details they, as journalists, were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In accordance with that, did you register all the POWs in accordance with the service rules on registering and listing the POWs once they were captured?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the registration of the POWs, we worked in accordance with the service rules. Whether we registered all the POWs as I noted when answering one of the Prosecutor's questions, I'm not certain whether all POWs were registered, and I cannot claim and say with 100 per cent certitude, that all POWs who were at the football field were listed and registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Malinic. On page 43 of today's transcript, in line 3, Mr. Vanderpuye asked you whether you contacted General Miletic. My question is this: Did you discuss the alleged telegram which you were supposed to receive from Savcic with Mr. Miletic, or did you discuss other problems and issues because he was at the operations centre? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of time has passed since 1995. Many events from my military career and my personal life have been such that I do not remember, first of all, whether I talked to General Miletic and, if so, what we talked about. If we did, whether we discussed the telegram or the situation in the territory of Nova Kasaba, I cannot say anything about this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P125, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Once it comes up on the screen, I'm showing it just for the record so that we could show what we are talking about. You will see on the screen what the Prosecutor showed you. I'm only interested in the following. Did you receive a telegram which was supposed to have the contents that this typed document but unsigned and unregistered document has? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, and from this point in time, I cannot say either yes or no. I don't remember if I received this telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As you see the telegram now and as you were an officer a long time, could the soldier who is in charge of decoding receive a telegram which has not been registered and which is not signed, if one were to investigate a crime, would you ask these questions to the decoder: Why did you receive a telegram which has not been signed and which has not been registered? Would he be allowed to do that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the rules on correspondence, the decoder should not receive any document which is not signed and which was sent by code because anyone could write a document and then sign someone else or include contents which have nothing do with the person who is sending that, whether he would be held criminally responsible or not, this is something I wouldn't know. I don't know enough about soldiers and officers who are in charge of working with codes, so this information could rather be provided by people who were serving in the communications units and who were in charge of encryption.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As a policeman, if you had seen such a telegram which is typed up but has not been sent by a teleprinter, what would you say in your report? Was it sent to a unit which perhaps may have perished because it never received this? If someone submitted to you a paper like this without perforated tape that would show that it was sent by a teleprinter, what would you write in your report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would write that a document is of doubtful origin and that there is no confirmation that the document was really sent for coding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So as not to waste any more time, on page 32, the Prosecutor asked you whether you knew that Egbers had come to see you and that when he came to see you, he stood there at gunpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show document P1143.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So that we could see how guns were pointed at him when he came to see you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1143, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do object to General Tolimir's question in the sense that it mischaracterises the question that I put to the witness. I did not tell the witness that Egbers came to him and he was at gunpoint. I said he was stopped at gunpoint before he came to him. And that's an important issue, I think, and it's an important fact for General Tolimir not to misrepresent to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Tolimir. Would you say that what you've just said reflects the -- what is written on page 32, that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read out what I wrote down in my notes: "Did you know that Egbers, before seeing you, was held at gunpoint?" This is what I noted down. I don't know whether I wrote everything correctly. But that's what I heard. In any case, whatever Mr. Vanderpuye said, I accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at paragraph 162, please. Before that, I need to say that this is an interview given by Egbers in 1997. Let's look at paragraph 162. Page 18, paragraph 162. The second paragraph. Apologies, my mistake. P1145, page 5. This is Egbers's statement, because I wanted to refer to both documents. So as not to waste any time, let's have a look at what Egbers says in paragraph 145. We can see his statement. Let's look at the penultimate paragraph: "On return, Lutke and I were stopped by Bosnian Serb soldiers. I saw a barracks ahead. A soldier pointed a gun at our vehicle. He ordered me to get out. I saw some ten of our men who had accompanied a convoy at the barricade. A soldier noted my name next to the road where the others were who had also been escorting a convoy. I asked to speak to a responsible officer. An hour later, I was taken to a small school." My question is this: Is it customary for check-point soldiers to stop all those approaching, with weapons, because they don't know if someone is an UNPROFOR member until that person shows their ID, or if someone else just put on a UN uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules of manning check-points is regulated either by the rules of service or separate order. And the basic rule is that if a check-point was set up, then there must be a specific task, due to which the check-point was set up and what the tasks of those manning it are. A check-point may serve different functions. First and foremost, it is usually to control vehicles and persons moving along a certain route. And military policemen are authorised to check the IDs of all those stopped at the check-point. They can also search them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Malinic. Let us correct my mistake from before. Let's look at P1143, which is Egbers's interview, paragraph 145 we saw a moment ago. In the preceding paragraphs, he described how he came to see you in that particular facility. Then he says that some orders must have been issued by your battalion to take care of the UN personnel and I asked him --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please specify where he is reading from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Tolimir, General Tolimir, could you tell us from where exactly you are reading? This would facilitate the task of the interpreters. Could you just tell us from where, from which position in the text you are reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was reading paragraphs 145 and 146.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The quote is: "I did have that impression. At a certain point, that school was attacked by the Muslims, two Muslims. I think no more than that [sic]."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not understand your question because I was busy reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: Was the school attacked while the UNPROFOR members were in it, as Mr. Egbers said?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately following their arrival in the barracks, there was an attack by the Muslim forces on the school, or the barracks, where some officers and soldiers were. That is where the UNPROFOR soldiers were at that moment as well, when the attack began.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In paragraph 149 that we see here, the question was: "Was it really a suicide attack by these two men?" And in paragraph 150, he says: "Yes, indeed. Or they thought, Let's first shoot a little and then get away quickly. That is also possible, of course. We don't know that. Well, I don't know anything else about that." My question is this: Did you repel the attack and did you protect the UNPROFOR members and the unit that was in the facility?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, I think what we read before that is also important, which is that Lieutenant Egbers assessed that these were two Muslim soldiers who attacked the school with small-calibre weapons. I don't know why he concluded there were two, and if he actually saw them, because the area where the attack came from was in the woods, and he had no possibility of seeing anyone from where he was. He simply couldn't see the situation. As for his statement that I took two prisoners and pushed them in front of me, is a lie. He said himself that he didn't participate in that skirmish. He returned and did not take any active participation. And, yet, a flew lines before that, he said that I was pushing the two prisoners in front of me as a human shield, without participating in the action. It's nonsensical. First of all, I don't know where his assessment comes from that these were two Muslims firing at the barracks and that they had small-calibre weapons. Also, you asked me about this part, where he says that he didn't know if it was a suicide attack or an actual attempt to break through the blockade line at that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, please. I did not want to interrupt the witness, but I wanted to tell the French booth that I can no longer hear the French interpretation. I haven't heard it for a while, so I don't know if it can be corrected. You may continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please have P857. We have seen it today. It's a satellite image, number 2 of Kasaba. I don't know what its exact number is that it was admitted under. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: In these yellow circles, is that people who are inside?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know the size of the pitch, or can you tell us how many people could have been there at 2.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I look at the size of the pitch and the size of the two rectangles, it would be my conclusion that at the pitch in Nova Kasaba at 2.00 p.m., there were up to 3- or 400 prisoners. By means at the disposal of this Tribunal, I'm pretty certain that an accurate calculation could be made as to the number of prisoners, if we take into account the size of the rectangles and compare that to the size of the pitch. I believe it can be precisely determined what the number of prisoners was. We can even measure the pitch as it is today, so as to know what its exact size is and compare that to the size of the two rectangles. I believe that it would be a calculation that could be as high as 95 per cent accurate as to the number of people in Kasaba on that day at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So as not to have to calculate that, can you tell us how many prisoners boarded those buses, since they were all registered? Actually, the military police unit carried out their registration.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise how many prisoners were put on the buses on the 13th of July in the afternoon. But I think the number was between 1.000 and 1.200. As for the lists of captured soldiers, they were handed over to the regiment command. It is clear on those lists who the people captured were, when they were captured, and whether they had any documents with them or not, personal documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you mentioned the regimental command, can you tell us whether the command was familiar with the incident in which one of the prisoners was killed in -- on the field?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The regimental command was informed of the incident, when the prisoner was killed at the field in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we have 15 minutes left, let me ask you this, which is something I forgot to ask you about Egbers. Did he leave the Mercedes vehicles behind or did you seize them from him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Egbers received an approval from his superior command to go back to the base in Potocari. In order to protect his personnel from being exposed to any gun-fire along the way, it was for that reason that he came to my office. He gave me the keys to the vehicles, and just before leaving, and before he brought the keys, he personally received a rifle from me as a souvenir so that he would remember his stay in Nova Kasaba. Something else I wanted to say about Lieutenant Egbers. Since he was constantly in touch with his command, it might be useful to try and locate any conversations he had with his command and the reports he sent on the 13th, 14th, and 15th of July. He had an overview of the entire situation at that time. Based on his statement, and I can see he gave it on September 2, 1999, which is four years later, I think the most credible source would be to check his reports to his command while he was in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you just said that, I now need to go back to P1143, which is Mr. Egbers's statement. He mentions the very fact in paragraph 162, paragraph 2, and paragraphs 163 and 164. We can see it here. In paragraph 142, he says -- we're reading from the sixth line in paragraph 145.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please provide exact reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My mistake. Paragraph 162; 162, not 145.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter in the French booth apologies. There seems to be a technical problem. It's not working.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can see it now in the English but not in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 of paragraph 162, "In my view," et cetera, "I knew the situation," I'll skip that: "I had driven along the road. I knew what there was along that road. I was worried about the safety of my own troops. I proposed once again exactly that we all go in an armoured vehicle of the Bosnian Serbs and that we disable the two vehicles and leave them behind. Franken gave us permission for this." In paragraph 163 the question is: "Did you get Franken personally on the line?" Paragraph 164: "Yes, it was Franken himself. But that went via Satcom. You type it in." My question is this: Did I quote correctly, and is what Mr. Egbers said correct, which is that he disabled the vehicles and handed you the keys?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only took the communication equipment from the two vehicles. I don't know much about it because their technology was very up to date and much more modern than ours. In any case, he took that equipment with him and the vehicles were not disabled. They functioned properly. When the UN forces were leaving Potocari, no one came back for those vehicles because they were handed over to me and a certificate -- a receipt was issued against it. Later on, the vehicles were used for the needs of the battalion and the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 51 of yesterday's transcript of the 8th of June, in line 12, you say that you were transferred to Serbia via Klagenfurt, and then to Sarajevo after you escaped from Varazdin. Can you explain that situation to us, and were you transferred or expelled to Slovenia and Austria, and in what way were you returned to your home country through different countries?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was taken prisoner at the Trinaesti Maj Barracks, where I was serving in the military police battalion as the assistant commander for morale, together with a group of other officers from the military police, these were four officers from this service. Two soldiers who worked in the military police service, and one lieutenant with two APCs, I think that these were the BVP M80 type. That was the composition of the group in the barracks. The barracks had been moved out, but as the Yugoslav People's Army, we had received an order not to surrender any army facility to anyone. Once we were captured by the ZNG troops, they kept us at a hunter's lodge, or a mountaineer's lodge, where they questioned us and where our former colleagues from state security interviewed the officers. People were taken out to be shot, but it turned out that these were not actual executions by firing squad but that this was just a stage show. After several days through Ormoz, we were transported to Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please. Overlapping speakers. We cannot interpret at this rate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I just wanted to have the witness say for the record from which country were they transported to Slovenia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was the crossing at Ormoz where state security forces of Slovenia immediately came and continued to question the soldiers and officers who were transported there. It lasted for one or two days, and those had been my colleagues, up until the previous day, in military police and who had joined the Slovenian police, took part in the questioning. As my acquaintance is from Slovenia, I called him, and in his vehicle from Ormoz, he took me to the boarder with Austria, where, in Austria, I got on a plane and I came to Sarajevo, and after that, I returned to Belgrade. There was no possibility of having other transport because the whole road was blocked. You couldn't travel overland in the direction of Bosnia or Serbia because all roads had been closed down. This was the only possibility to reach Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But you have not answered my question. As a member of the Yugoslav People's Army, once you were captured in Vukovar in Croatia, were you exported to a foreign country, and did you return to your home country from that foreign country later on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think it was wasn't Vukovar but, rather, Varazdin. Yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 51, you also talked about those who were killed in the hospital in Sarajevo, those from your unit. Can you tell us whether you know what was the total number of those who were killed, both in Dobrovoljacka Street and in the other location which you described? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say how many dead from the detachment there were. That happened on 2nd of May, 1992. And as for the incident in Dobrovoljacka Street, that was on the 3rd of May, 1992. Perhaps I could quote or, rather, tell you from my memory what the media carried; that there were more than 40 dead on the whole, taking both the 2nd and the 3rd of May. I mean the dead members of the JNA in Dobrovoljacka Street and at Skenderija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us whether you were also attacked in Croatia by forces who were not constitutionally legitimate and legalised as armed forces at the time. Did the same thing also happen in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and was the JNA attacked by paramilitary formations in these two republics?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I worked in Croatia, when I discharged the duty as the military police battalion commander, we had much co-operation with their anti-terrorist unit which was attached to the Croatian MUP. As they could do not do some exercises, like shooting from a helicopter which was part of their training, then they did this exercise together with members of my unit at the Slunj training ground. At the time, in Croatia, great pressure was excerpted on members of the military police. Officers were offered money to cross over to them and train their army, which was being established but which was not legitimate and it was not legal. They offered money. If you refused -- just for you to leave the JNA and leave Croatia. Some officers, whether it was due to pressure because of their families which live there, accepted such deals. I was personally threatened in Varazdin that they would kill my family because they knew where I lived and where my family was. I experienced such things from people I had worked together with until recently. Such things also happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, once the unit went there. In the beginning, our main task was to set up a military police -- or, rather, the military police battalion, and the protection regiment had the task to form mixed patrol units with the local MUP which functioned in the beginning. Later on, the police split along ethnic lines, and such units no longer existed; I mean, the joint patrol units no longer existed in the city. There was sporadic shooting in Sarajevo, sporadic fire from various sides. And, as for the outbreak of war, the 22nd of April can be taken as the date, as 12 people were killed by Muslim forces when they were attacked in the area of the Hotel Srbija. The Yugoslav People's Army got involved, and the first units which came out to the ground came out into the territory of Ilidza municipality. This is what I know about the outbreak of the war there. There are many issues that we could also discuss in relation with this, but I think that -- I'm not sure whether time will allow us to do that, to discuss the incidents where the attacks on the JNA occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. General Tolimir, I realise that it is 13 hours and 47 minutes, so we will undoubtedly not be able to finish today, since we have no more time. I assume you haven't finished. Please put your microphone on because I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I tried to speed up, to finish my examination so that the witness wouldn't sit here and wait for a week. So if you would allow Mr. Vanderpuye to ask additional questions, I think I did not move out of the framework of cross-examination so that the witness wouldn't have to wait. I have no further questions. I just need to ask the witness, because he said that he was falsely accused of certain crimes, if he wanted to tell us something about that. Because it is my duty to ask him this. And, if necessary, we might move to -- do you agree that by 12.00 Mr. Vanderpuye should finish, if I could reduce my cross-examination to 45 minutes, then he might reduce his additional re-examination to 15 minutes and then we might release this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Tolimir, why are you finishing your cross-examination now, since you still have enough time, and you have not had or used your three-hour allotted time? You feel you wish to end your cross-examination now. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President. I believe that we should finish everything today so that the witness would not have to wait another five days for another 15 minutes. This is what I did, and I don't mind it if you don't mind. Thank you. I would just ask one additional question and then I would end my examination. I would just like to give the witness a chance to answer that one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead and put your additional question, in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My additional question is this: Do you feel any need to say anything about false accusations which were made against you earlier and which caused you certain problems? If you don't wish to do that in open session, we might move to private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the statement which I gave at the ICTY office in Belgrade, I said everything, because the Prosecutor, or, rather, the investigator, told me that I had committed a war crime and why did General Krstic point his finger at me as someone who had committed a war crime. I answered that that was not a question for me, but, rather, for General Krstic. Namely, what were the reasons why he mentioned not just me but also the unit which I commanded, and what made him say that. Was it the position where we were, shifting the burden of guilt to a unit which was not part of the Drina Corps? Maybe that was the reason for justifying his own activities. I really couldn't say what his reasons for that may have been. I was very surprised by the fact when it was mentioned in the media. I had no opportunity, nor did this Tribunal ever call me before 2005 to give any sort of statement about the events which took place in the relevant period in Nova Kasaba. I do have my opinion about all this, but I rather wouldn't state it here before the Tribunal. It's a personal matter which remains such. I wouldn't like to state any counteraccusations against anyone or blame anyone for incidents that I do not know much about and that I'm not certain about. That is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Malinic. Thank you for coming here. God bless you. Thank you for coming here, and I wish you happy return home.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN MALINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too. I wish you much health, a long life, and I hope you will manage to defend yourself by using arguments before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is what the Defence had to ask this witness. Perhaps he could be re-examined here so that he could go home and wouldn't have to wait another five days for 15 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir, for your cross-examination. Mr. Prosecutor, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do have a few questions, and I see that we've got about -- we're overtime, actually, I think. And the nature of the examination is relatively short, which I don't think it would be worth keeping him here for a long time to deal with. This is unfortunate, because General Tolimir had estimated three hours, I think, which obviously would have required the witness returning, in any event, whereby, I would be able to conduct a, at least, effective re-direct examination. But I don't think I can do that in this amount of time. So I leave it to your discretion. I don't know what the witness's schedule is like to determine whether or not he should continue on Tuesday. If his inclination is that he has to leave and he can't be here Tuesday because of family commitments, work commitments, or some other reason, and that's fine with the Court, then I will abide by that. But, otherwise, I would like to ask him just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How much time would you need to ask those questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't think much more than five or ten minutes. Obviously it depends on the length of his answers. But not more than five or ten minutes. But I see that we don't have that, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, could you be here on Tuesday once again, because ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If need be, and if I have to, I'll stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, once you allow me to leave, I wait for Radovan Karadzic, because he stays up until 3.00 p.m. every day. So if only ten or 15 minutes are needed, can't we prolong this for ten or 15 minutes to save something for the Tribunal and so that this man wouldn't have to stay here another five days because there would be a five-day break? This is why I tried to speed up my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. Well, as you can see, the Chamber is made up of two Judges today. We cannot continue because Judge Nyambe has other arrangements that should begin very soon. Therefore, we have to adjourn and we will resume on Tuesday. The session is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of June, 2011, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.56 p.m.,
